claim: Pacific parrotlets exhibit stereotyped leg and wing dynamics regardless of perch diameter and texture.
source: Here, we show how Pacific parrotlets exhibit stereotyped leg and wing dynamics regardless of perch diameter and texture, but foot, toe, and claw kinematics become surface-specific upon touchdown.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing similar landing force trends across different perches (Figure 2).

claim: Foot, toe, and claw kinematics become surface-specific upon touchdown.
source: Here, we show how Pacific parrotlets exhibit stereotyped leg and wing dynamics regardless of perch diameter and texture, but foot, toe, and claw kinematics become surface-specific upon touchdown.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by kinematic data showing divergence in foot and claw angles after contact (Figure 3C).

claim: Birds combine predictable toe pad friction with probabilistic friction from their claws.
source: They combine predictable toe pad friction with probabilistic friction from their claws, which they drag to find surface asperities—dragging further when they can squeeze less.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by friction testing data showing toe pads follow Coulomb friction while claws show greater variability (Figure 4).

claim: Birds drag their claws to find surface asperities, dragging further when they can squeeze less.
source: They combine predictable toe pad friction with probabilistic friction from their claws, which they drag to find surface asperities—dragging further when they can squeeze less.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing increased claw curling on surfaces that are harder to squeeze (Figure 3G, H).

claim: Parrotlet claws can undergo superfast movements within 1–2 ms on moderately slippery surfaces.
source: Remarkably, parrotlet claws can undergo superfast movements, within 1–2 ms, on moderately slippery surfaces to find more secure asperities when necessary.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by high-speed video analysis showing claw movements occurring in 1-2 ms (Figure 3F).

claim: Birds first ramp up safety margins by squeezing before relaxing their grasp.
source: With this strategy, they first ramp up safety margins by squeezing before relaxing their grasp.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by force data showing squeeze forces and safety margins peak later and decay more slowly than body forces (Figure 6D-F).

claim: It is advantageous to be small for stable perching when high friction relative to normal force is required because claws can find more usable surface.
source: The model further shows it is advantageous to be small for stable perching when high friction relative to normal force is required because claws can find more usable surface, but this trend reverses when required friction shrinks.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by traced surface modeling showing smaller tip radii have more usable surface at high friction requirements (Figure 5F).

claim: The advantage of being small for stable perching reverses when required friction shrinks.
source: The model further shows it is advantageous to be small for stable perching when high friction relative to normal force is required because claws can find more usable surface, but this trend reverses when required friction shrinks.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by traced surface modeling showing the trend flattens or reverses at lower friction requirements (Figure 5F).

claim: Aerial robots still lack the versatility and robustness that birds exhibit when landing on complex surfaces.
source: However, they still lack the versatility and robustness that birds exhibit when landing on an extraordinarily wide range of complex engineered and natural surfaces (Kovac, 2016; Roderick et al., 2017a; Doyle et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous studies have quantified leg and wing dynamics during bird landings.
source: Previous studies have quantified leg and wing dynamics (Provini et al., 2012; Provini et al., 2014; Chin and Lentink, 2017; Provini and Abourachid, 2018) and suggested visual control strategies (Chin and Lentink, 2017; Lee et al., 1993) that arboreal birds use during landings.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous studies have suggested visual control strategies that arboreal birds use during landings.
source: Previous studies have quantified leg and wing dynamics (Provini et al., 2012; Provini et al., 2014; Chin and Lentink, 2017; Provini and Abourachid, 2018) and suggested visual control strategies (Chin and Lentink, 2017; Lee et al., 1993) that arboreal birds use during landings.
evidence: The claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: It is unclear whether previous findings on bird landing dynamics would apply with perches that have different geometric properties and challenging surface textures.
source: However, it is unclear whether the same findings would apply with perches that have different geometric properties and challenging surface textures.

claim: Previous studies have examined the morphology of bird feet in cadavers.
